idiom_name: impl From<A> for B / impl From<B> for A, with TryFrom or FromStr for parsing
implementation_notes: Rust ships the pattern as conversion traits: From is the reciprocal of Into (implementing From provides Into for free), so a pair of impl From<A> for B and impl From<B> for A placed in the modules that own each type is the language's bidirectional mapping, and neither type needs the other's module. The orphan rule forces the impls to live where a local type is involved, which is exactly the decoupling the pattern asks for; From is infallible and lossless by contract, so parsing and validation belong to TryFrom/FromStr. A converter struct with two methods is still justified when the mapping must be selected at runtime or shared as a value.
pitfalls: From must be infallible and lossless: fallible or lossy mappings (parsing text, narrowing integers) belong in TryFrom/FromStr, and using as casts for them silently truncates.
The orphan rule blocks impl From between two foreign types; a local newtype is the only legal way to own that mapping.
Both directions must be checked for symmetry - i64 to u64 to i64 is not safe for negative input, so a round-trip test is mandatory.

variants.name: serde Serialize/Deserialize derive with rename attributes
variants.implementation_notes: When the second representation is a wire or storage format, serde's derive generates both directions from one declaration - Serialize (value to format) and Deserialize (format to value) - while the format crate (serde_json, bincode, toml) supplies the rest, so the two sides never name each other. #[serde(into = "...", try_from = "...")] routes through an existing From/TryFrom impl when the derived shape is wrong, and #[serde(with = module)] handles a shape serde cannot express by itself.
variants.code_sketch:
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct TicketDto {
    pub id: u64,
    #[serde(rename = "created_at")]
    pub created_at: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub active: bool,
}

let wire = serde_json::to_string(&dto)?;             // Serialize
let back: TicketDto = serde_json::from_str(&wire)?;   // Deserialize
pitfalls: The derive couples the type to the wire contract: renaming a field changes the format unless #[serde(rename)] pins it, and adding a field breaks readers unless #[serde(default)] is set.
Unknown fields are ignored unless deny_unknown_fields is set, which hides producer-side drift that a strict contract would catch.
The derive feature and a format crate are required, so no_std or hand-rolled formats need manual impls.
Serialize and Deserialize are independent impls - a custom serializer without a matching deserializer breaks the round trip.
